q: The tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain toxoids. A toxoid is:
o: A live bacterium with its toxin gene removed
A bacterial toxin made harmless by treatment but still able to stimulate antibody production
An antibody made against the toxin in a horse
A synthetic antibiotic that destroys the toxin
x: Toxoids are toxins inactivated, for example with formaldehyde, so they no longer cause harm but keep their antigenic shape. The body makes antibodies (antitoxins) and memory cells against them.

q: Edward Jenner made the first vaccine against smallpox by using material from:
x: In 1796 Jenner inoculated a boy with material from cowpox sores; the mild cowpox virus protected him against the related smallpox virus. Smallpox is caused by a virus, not a bacterium.

q: Louis Pasteur developed attenuated vaccines, including one against:
x: Pasteur weakened (attenuated) pathogens in the laboratory and produced vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies. The smallpox vaccine came from Jenner, and polio and measles vaccines came in the twentieth century.

q: Viruses used in traditional live attenuated vaccines are usually weakened by:
o: Treating them with formaldehyde until they are dead
Growing them repeatedly in cell cultures or animals until they lose their virulence
Mixing them with antibodies from a recovered patient
x: Repeated growth in culture selects variants that multiply well in the laboratory but cause little or no disease in humans. Formaldehyde treatment kills the virus, which gives an inactivated vaccine, not an attenuated one.

q: The MMR vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella is an example of a:
o: Recombinant subunit vaccine made in yeast
x: MMR contains weakened but living measles, mumps and rubella viruses. Toxoids are used against bacterial toxins such as tetanus, and the yeast-made subunit vaccine is the hepatitis B vaccine.

q: For producing vaccines, influenza and some other viruses are grown in large numbers in:
o: Fertilised hen's eggs or cultures of living cells
x: Viruses multiply only inside living cells, so they are grown in embryonated (fertilised) eggs or in animal cell cultures. Nutrient agar supports bacteria and fungi, not viruses.

q: Viruses for vaccine production cannot be grown on nutrient media like bacteria because they:
o: Are too large to fit on a culture plate
Can reproduce only inside living host cells
Are killed by the oxygen in air
Need sunlight to make their own food
x: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: they have no metabolism of their own and use the host cell's machinery to multiply. They are far smaller than bacteria.

q: For large-scale production of a recombinant vaccine protein, the genetically modified yeast cells are grown in:
x: Fermenters provide the right temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients so the engineered microbes multiply and make the protein in large amounts. Eggs are used for growing viruses, not yeast.

q: After genetically modified yeast cells have made the viral surface protein for a vaccine, the next stage of production is to:
o: Inject the yeast cells directly into people
Insert the protein gene into a plasmid
Cut the yeast DNA with restriction enzymes
Break open the cells and purify the protein
x: Downstream processing separates the wanted protein from the yeast cells and their other contents, giving a pure antigen for the vaccine. Inserting the gene and cutting DNA are earlier steps.

q: A rare risk of the oral (Sabin) polio vaccine is that:
o: It contains toxins that damage the liver
It makes people allergic to all other vaccines
It causes antibodies to attack the person's own nerves
The weakened virus may mutate back to a form that can cause paralysis
x: Because the oral vaccine contains live attenuated virus, in very rare cases the virus mutates and regains its ability to cause paralysis. This risk does not exist with the inactivated (Salk) vaccine.

q: An 'edible vaccine' is produced by:
o: Mixing killed bacteria into ordinary food
Drying a live vaccine and adding it to sugar
Inserting a gene for a pathogen's antigen into a food plant so its tissues make the antigen
x: In edible vaccines a transgenic plant, such as potato or banana, expresses an antigen of a pathogen. Eating the plant tissue could then stimulate immunity without injection.

q: An mRNA vaccine, such as some COVID-19 vaccines, protects against the virus by:
o: Inserting the whole viral genome into human chromosomes
Delivering ready-made antibodies against the virus
Supplying mRNA that body cells use to make a viral protein, which the immune system then responds to
Containing live weakened virus that multiplies in the body
x: The mRNA is translated by the person's own cells into the viral spike protein, which acts as an antigen and triggers antibodies and memory cells. The mRNA does not enter the chromosomes, and no live virus is given.

q: In a viral-vector vaccine, a harmless virus is used to:
o: Carry a gene for an antigen of another pathogen into body cells
x: The vector virus is modified so it cannot cause disease, and it carries a gene for the target pathogen's antigen. Body cells make that antigen, which stimulates an immune response.

q: The name of the restriction enzyme EcoRI shows that it was first isolated from:
x: Restriction enzymes are named after the bacterium they come from: 'Eco' stands for Escherichia coli, 'R' for the strain and 'I' because it was the first enzyme found in that strain.

q: Some restriction enzymes cut both strands of DNA at exactly the same point. The fragments produced have:
o: Blunt ends with no unpaired bases
x: A straight cut through both strands gives blunt ends. Sticky ends arise only when the enzyme makes staggered cuts, leaving short single-stranded overhangs.

q: A linear DNA molecule contains three recognition sites for a particular restriction enzyme. Complete digestion with this enzyme will give how many fragments?
x: Each cut in a linear molecule adds one more piece, so three cuts give four fragments. A circular plasmid with three sites would give only three fragments.

q: Plasmids and a donor gene are both cut with EcoRI and mixed with DNA ligase. Besides recombinant plasmids, which other product is commonly formed?
o: Plasmids that have rejoined their own ends without taking up the gene
Proteins coded by the donor gene
x: The sticky ends of a cut plasmid can pair with each other, so some plasmids simply close up again without the gene. This is why bacteria must be screened afterwards to find those with the recombinant plasmid.

q: After transformation, bacteria are spread on agar containing an antibiotic. The plasmid carries a resistance gene for that antibiotic. Bacteria that did NOT take up any plasmid will:
o: Fail to grow, because they are killed by the antibiotic
Grow and make the foreign protein
x: Only bacteria carrying the plasmid have the resistance gene, so only they survive on the antibiotic plate. Untransformed bacteria are killed, which allows the transformed ones to be selected.

q: A plasmid carries genes for resistance to ampicillin and tetracycline. A foreign gene is inserted into the middle of the tetracycline-resistance gene. Bacteria carrying this recombinant plasmid will:
o: Grow on tetracycline but not on ampicillin
Grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline
x: Inserting the gene into the tetracycline-resistance gene disrupts it (insertional inactivation), so those bacteria become sensitive to tetracycline. The ampicillin-resistance gene is untouched, so they still grow on ampicillin.

q: In genetic engineering, 'gene cloning' means:
o: Producing a whole new animal from a body cell
Changing the base sequence of a gene at random
Making many identical copies of a gene by letting host cells that contain it multiply
Cutting a gene into many small pieces
x: Each time a transformed bacterium divides, its recombinant plasmid is copied, so a colony holds millions of copies of the inserted gene. Producing a whole animal from a body cell is reproductive cloning, a different process.

q: When a high proportion of people in a community are vaccinated against measles, even unvaccinated babies are better protected. This is because:
o: The vaccine spreads from vaccinated people to the babies
Vaccinated people pass their memory cells to babies by touch
The virus cannot spread easily through a mostly immune population
The measles virus becomes harmless after a vaccination campaign
x: When most people are immune, an infected person meets few susceptible contacts, so chains of transmission break. This is called herd immunity. The vaccine itself is not passed to others.

q: After vaccination, the antibodies themselves are secreted by:
o: Plasma cells developed from B lymphocytes
x: Antigen in the vaccine activates B lymphocytes, which divide and form plasma cells that secrete antibodies, as well as memory B cells. Neutrophils engulf microbes but do not make antibodies.

q: The only human disease that has so far been eradicated worldwide through vaccination is:
x: After a global vaccination campaign, smallpox was declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980. Polio still persists in a few countries, including Pakistan.

q: A labelled RNA probe for a particular gene's mRNA is applied to a slice of tissue and gives a strong signal. This shows that in that tissue the gene is:
x: The probe binds to mRNA, and mRNA is present only when the gene is being transcribed. All body cells carry the gene, but only cells expressing it contain its mRNA.

q: Which base is found in an RNA probe but not in a DNA probe?
x: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Adenine and guanine (and cytosine) are found in both DNA and RNA.

q: A DNA probe with the sequence 5'-TACG-3' is used to detect an mRNA. The complementary mRNA sequence it pairs with is:
x: T pairs with A, A with U (RNA has no T), C with G and G with C, and the strands run antiparallel. So the mRNA reads 3'-AUGC-5'. A sequence containing T cannot be mRNA.

q: After a radioactively labelled probe has hybridised with DNA on a membrane, its position is usually revealed by:
o: Placing the membrane against X-ray film (autoradiography)
Examining it under a light microscope only
x: Radiation from the bound probe darkens photographic or X-ray film, showing bands where the target sequence is. Fluorescent probes are seen under suitable light instead.

q: After a labelled probe is added to the sample DNA, any probe that has not paired is washed off. This is done so that:
o: Any signal left comes only from probe bound to the target sequence
The sample DNA is copied many times
The probe is converted into protein
x: Washing removes loose probe; only probe held by complementary base pairing remains. A signal then shows that the target sequence is present in the sample.

q: In Southern blotting, DNA fragments separated by gel electrophoresis are transferred to a membrane and then:
o: Tested with a labelled probe to find a particular sequence
x: Blotting fixes the separated fragments on a membrane; a labelled probe then shows which band contains the target sequence. Ligase joins DNA rather than cutting it.

q: Fetal DNA is tested with two probes. The probe for the sickle-cell allele binds, but the probe for the normal haemoglobin allele does not. The fetus is:
x: Since only the sickle-cell probe binds, the fetus has no normal allele and two sickle-cell alleles. A carrier would bind both probes; a normal homozygote would bind only the normal probe.

q: For prenatal diagnosis of a genetic disorder with DNA probes, fetal cells are usually obtained by:
o: Taking a blood sample from the father
Testing the mother's urine for hCG
Collecting cells from the mother's mouth
x: Amniocentesis collects fetal cells from the amniotic fluid, and chorionic villus sampling takes cells from the developing placenta. Both provide fetal DNA; the father's or mother's own cells do not.

q: A DNA probe test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum is valuable mainly because:
o: It gives a result quickly, whereas culturing these slow-growing bacteria takes weeks
It kills the bacteria in the sample
It works without any bacterial DNA being present
It is a vaccine as well as a test
x: Tuberculosis bacteria grow very slowly, so culture can take several weeks. A probe detects their DNA directly, allowing much quicker diagnosis and treatment.

q: Which set of temperatures matches the three steps of a PCR cycle (denaturation, primer annealing, extension) in that order?
x: DNA strands separate at about 95 °C, primers bind at about 50–60 °C and Taq polymerase extends them at about 72 °C, its optimum. The cycle then repeats.

q: Which of the following is NOT added to a PCR reaction mixture?
x: PCR needs template DNA, two primers, the four nucleotides and a heat-stable polymerase in buffer. Ligase joins DNA fragments in gene cloning and is not used to copy DNA in PCR.

q: Starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, what is the smallest number of PCR cycles needed to obtain at least 1000 copies of the target?
x: The amount doubles every cycle, giving 2ⁿ copies after n cycles. 2⁹ = 512 is too few, while 2¹⁰ = 1024 is the first value above 1000.

q: The RT-PCR test used to diagnose COVID-19 first uses the enzyme reverse transcriptase because:
o: The virus has a protein coat that must be digested
Human DNA must be removed before testing
The virus's genetic material is RNA, which must be copied into DNA before PCR
Primers can bind only to protein
x: PCR copies DNA, but the coronavirus genome is RNA. Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA from the viral RNA, which is then amplified and detected.

q: After the fusion step in monoclonal antibody production, each hybridoma clone is tested (screened) in order to:
o: Remove the antigen from the mouse
Find the clone that makes antibody against the required antigen
x: The B cells from the spleen make many different antibodies, so clones are screened and only the one producing antibody to the chosen antigen is grown on a large scale.

q: In the ELISA test, used for example to detect HIV infection, an antibody is linked to an enzyme so that:
o: The virus in the sample is destroyed
The antibody can enter the patient's cells
A colour change shows that the target has been bound
x: When the enzyme-linked antibody is bound in the test well, adding the enzyme's substrate produces a coloured product. The colour indicates the presence of the antigen or antibody being tested for.

q: In blood banks, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
o: Destroy all bacteria in donated blood
Increase the number of red cells in stored blood
Copy the DNA of blood donors
Identify blood group antigens such as A, B and Rh accurately
x: Monoclonal antibodies against the A, B and Rh antigens are highly specific and uniform, so they give reliable blood-grouping results. They do not sterilise blood or copy DNA.

q: In a pregnancy test strip, the test line turns coloured when hCG is present because:
o: hCG itself is coloured and sticks to the strip
hCG attached to coloured, mobile antibodies is trapped by fixed antibodies at the test line
Urine reacts with the strip to make hCG
The fixed antibodies change colour on contact with any urine
x: Mobile antibodies carrying a coloured label bind hCG and move up the strip; fixed antibodies at the test line capture the hCG–antibody complex, so colour builds up there. Without hCG the labelled antibodies pass on to the control line only.

q: Home ovulation-prediction kits use monoclonal antibodies to detect a rise in the urine level of:
x: A surge of LH triggers ovulation, so detecting it in urine shows that ovulation is about to occur. hCG is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.

q: DNA fingerprinting compares regions of DNA that:
o: Code for the same protein in every person
Are found only in red blood cells
Contain short sequences repeated a different number of times in different people
x: Non-coding regions with tandem repeats vary in the number of repeats between individuals, so cutting or amplifying them gives fragments of different lengths. This produces a band pattern unique to each person except identical twins.

q: In a paternity test using DNA profiles, every band in the child's profile should be present in:
o: Both the mother's and the father's profiles
Either the mother's profile or the true father's profile
x: A child inherits half its DNA from each parent, so each band comes from one parent or the other. Bands not found in the mother must match the true father.

q: Which pair correctly matches a technique with its use?
o: ELISA: detecting an antigen or antibody in a blood sample
PCR: separating DNA fragments by size
Gel electrophoresis: making millions of copies of DNA
DNA ligase: detecting a gene in a sample
x: ELISA uses enzyme-linked antibodies to detect antigens or antibodies. PCR amplifies DNA, gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size, and ligase joins DNA pieces.

q: In PCR, DNA polymerase cannot start making a new strand without a primer because it:
o: Can only add nucleotides to the free 3' end of an existing strand
Is destroyed at the annealing temperature
Needs the primer as an energy source
x: DNA polymerase extends an existing chain by adding nucleotides to its 3' end; it cannot begin a chain from nothing. The primers provide these starting 3' ends on each side of the target.

q: During gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, the smallest fragments:
o: Move farthest towards the positive electrode
x: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode. Small fragments slip through the gel more easily and travel farthest.

q: Recombinant human insulin is used in the treatment of:
x: Insulin lowers blood glucose and is given to people with diabetes mellitus whose bodies make too little insulin. Diabetes insipidus is due to lack of ADH, not insulin.

q: The first product of recombinant DNA technology approved for treating humans, in 1982, was:
x: Human insulin made by genetically engineered E. coli was approved in 1982, the first recombinant medicine. tPA, erythropoietin and recombinant clotting factors followed later.

q: In a later method of making recombinant insulin, bacteria produce a single chain, proinsulin. Proinsulin is converted to active insulin by:
o: Joining it to a second proinsulin chain
Adding a haem group to it
Using enzymes to cut out the connecting C-peptide
x: Proinsulin is one chain in which the two insulin chains are linked by a C-peptide. Enzymes remove this connecting piece, leaving the two insulin chains joined by disulphide bridges.

q: Monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat some cancers because they:
o: Bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells and can carry drugs to them or mark them for destruction
Copy the DNA of cancer cells
Replace the faulty gene in every body cell
Increase the division rate of all cells
x: A monoclonal antibody recognises one antigen on the cancer cell, so it can deliver an attached drug or toxin straight to it or flag it for the immune system, sparing most normal cells.

q: Monoclonal antibodies made entirely from mouse cells often stop working when given repeatedly to a patient because:
o: Mouse antibodies are too small to bind antigens
They are digested by the patient's red blood cells
The patient's immune system makes antibodies against the foreign mouse protein
They change into hormones in the human body
x: Mouse proteins are foreign to humans, so repeated doses trigger an immune response that destroys them. Scientists therefore make 'humanised' antibodies that are mostly human in structure.

q: The antibiotic penicillin is produced commercially by growing:
o: The fungus Penicillium in large fermenters
x: Penicillin is made by the mould Penicillium, grown in large fermenters under controlled conditions; the antibiotic is then extracted and purified.

q: Streptomycin, an antibiotic used against tuberculosis, is obtained from:
x: Streptomycin is produced by Streptomyces, a soil-dwelling bacterium that is a source of many antibiotics. Streptococcus is a pathogen and the source of streptokinase, not streptomycin.

q: Genetically modified goats and sheep have been used to produce human proteins for treatment, such as clotting proteins, by:
o: Releasing the protein in their urine as a hormone
Secreting the human protein in their milk
Storing the protein in their wool
Producing it in their red blood cells
x: The human gene is joined to a promoter that is active only in the mammary gland, so the protein is secreted into the milk, from which it is collected and purified. This is sometimes called pharming.

q: Streptokinase, an enzyme obtained from Streptococcus bacteria, is used medically to:
o: Dissolve blood clots, for example after a heart attack
x: Streptokinase activates the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin, so it breaks down clots blocking the coronary arteries. It is not an antibiotic.

q: tPA is helpful in a stroke caused by a blood clot but would be dangerous in a stroke caused by bleeding in the brain. The reason is that tPA:
o: Raises the blood glucose level sharply
Breaks down fibrin, so it would prevent bleeding from being stopped by clotting
x: tPA activates plasmin, which digests the fibrin of clots. In a bleeding stroke, clots are needed to seal the damaged vessel, so dissolving them would make the bleeding worse.

q: A harmless virus carrying a normal gene is injected straight into a patient's eye to treat an inherited form of blindness. This approach is described as:
x: The gene is delivered directly into body cells inside the patient, so it is in vivo; only somatic (eye) cells are changed, so it is not inherited. Ex vivo therapy treats cells outside the body and returns them.

q: Retroviruses have been used as vectors in some gene therapy because they:
o: Make proteins without using the host cell
Destroy the faulty gene in the patient
Insert their genetic material into the host cell's chromosomes
x: A retrovirus makes a DNA copy of its RNA and integrates it into the host's chromosome, so the inserted normal gene is copied each time the cell divides. It adds a working gene rather than destroying the faulty one.

q: Liposomes used to carry genes into cells in gene therapy are:
o: Modified bacteria that infect the lungs
Small circular DNA molecules from bacteria
Tiny spheres with a lipid bilayer that can fuse with cell membranes
x: A liposome is a small vesicle made of phospholipid bilayer; DNA packed inside it is delivered when the liposome fuses with the cell membrane. Small circular bacterial DNA molecules are plasmids.

q: Gene therapy is most suitable for treating disorders that are:
o: Caused by a defect in a single gene
Due to injuries such as fractures
x: Gene therapy adds a working copy of a gene, so it suits disorders such as cystic fibrosis or SCID that are caused by one faulty gene. Infections, injuries and diet-related problems are not gene defects.

q: The gene inserted in gene therapy for cystic fibrosis codes for:
o: A chloride-ion channel protein (CFTR) in cell membranes
x: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a faulty CFTR gene; the protein is a chloride channel, and its failure produces thick, sticky mucus. Adenosine deaminase is the enzyme missing in one form of SCID.

q: In the first gene therapy for ADA-deficient SCID, treatment had to be repeated every few months because:
o: The corrected white blood cells had a limited lifespan and were not stem cells
The patient's body destroyed the ADA enzyme in the blood
The gene was inserted into the patient's red blood cells
The bacteria used as vectors kept dying
x: The normal ADA gene was put into the patient's T lymphocytes, which die after some time. As they were not stem cells, new corrected cells were not produced, so fresh treated cells had to be given again.

q: Haemophilia B is treated with recombinant:
x: Haemophilia B results from a lack of clotting factor IX, whereas haemophilia A results from lack of factor VIII. Both can be treated with the correct recombinant clotting factor.

q: Which of the following medicines made by biotechnology is an enzyme?
x: tPA is a protease enzyme that converts plasminogen into plasmin. Insulin, growth hormone and erythropoietin are hormones, not enzymes.

q: Which recombinant product is used to PREVENT a disease rather than to treat it?
x: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is given to healthy people so they become immune before infection. Insulin, factor VIII and erythropoietin replace substances missing in people who already have a disorder.

q: Recombinant factor VIII and erythropoietin are usually produced in cultured mammalian cells rather than in bacteria because:
o: Mammalian cells multiply faster than bacteria
These proteins need modifications, such as added sugar groups, that bacteria cannot carry out
These proteins are poisonous to all bacteria
x: Many human proteins work properly only after processing such as glycosylation, which bacteria lack. Mammalian cells, for example hamster ovary cells, process them like human cells, though they grow more slowly than bacteria.

q: In some early gene therapy trials, a few patients developed leukaemia. The main reason was that:
o: The inserted gene coded for a cancer-causing toxin
The patients were given too much insulin
The viral vector inserted the gene next to a gene controlling cell division and switched it on
The liposomes caused the white cells to burst
x: Retroviral vectors insert their DNA at random places in the chromosomes. In these cases the insertion activated a gene that controls cell division, leading to uncontrolled growth of white blood cells.

q: Bacteria can make a correct human protein such as insulin from an inserted human gene (cDNA) because:
o: Bacteria and humans have identical chromosomes
The genetic code is universal, so they translate the gene the same way
The human gene changes into a bacterial gene
x: The same codons stand for the same amino acids in almost all organisms, so bacterial ribosomes produce the same amino acid sequence as human cells would from that gene.
